title: Jerusalem Spared from Assyria
overview: With the mighty Assyrian army threatening Jerusalem, King Hezekiah turns to God in prayer, the prophet Isaiah promises rescue, and the invaders suddenly withdraw.

parts.label: Hezekiah seeks Isaiah (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: Tearing his clothes and wearing sackcloth, a rough cloth worn in grief, showed the king's deep distress at Assyria's insults against God. Isaiah answers that the Assyrian king will hear a piece of news, go home, and die by the sword there.

parts.label: A threatening letter (vv. 8-13)
parts.note: Word that Tirhakah, a ruler from Cush (the region south of Egypt), was marching against him made Sennacherib want Jerusalem to surrender quickly. His letter lists cities Assyria had crushed, arguing that Judah's God will fail just as their gods did.

parts.label: Hezekiah's prayer (vv. 14-19)
parts.note: Hezekiah spreads the letter out in the temple, as if showing it to God. He admits Assyria's victories are real but says those gods were only carved wood and stone, and he asks for rescue so every nation will know the LORD alone is God.

parts.label: God answers the boaster (vv. 20-28)
parts.note: In this poem Jerusalem is pictured as a young woman shaking her head in scorn at a retreating enemy, while the Assyrian king brags of conquering mountains and drying up Egypt's rivers. God says Assyria succeeded only because he allowed it, and he will lead the king home like an animal with a hook in its nose.

parts.label: A sign and a promise (vv. 29-34)
parts.note: For two years the people would live on crops that grew wild, but in the third year normal farming would return, a sign that Judah would recover and grow again. The city would not even face an arrow or a siege ramp, because God would defend it for the sake of his promise to King David's family line.

parts.label: Assyria's collapse (vv. 35-37)
parts.note: The text says the angel of the LORD struck down 185,000 soldiers in one night, without giving any other cause; Assyrian records boast of trapping Hezekiah in Jerusalem but never claim to have taken the city. Sennacherib went home, and other ancient records confirm his sons later killed him, about twenty years afterward.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the overnight death of 185,000 soldiers should be read as a literal miracle exactly as described or as a theological telling of a real Assyrian withdrawal whose actual cause is unknown.
think: When you face something far bigger than yourself, where do you instinctively turn first, and what draws you there?
